site.sv.name: Silicon Valley
site.sv.what: Chip design, and the software chips are designed with. Many of the world's chips are specified and designed here, and several of the biggest makers of fab tools are based nearby.
site.sv.who: Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Synopsys, Cadence, Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA
site.sd.name: San Diego
site.sd.what: Qualcomm designs the chips inside many of the world's phones here.
site.sea.name: Seattle
site.sea.what: Home of two of the largest cloud companies, which now design their own chips for their data centres.
site.phx.name: Phoenix
site.phx.what: A new cluster of chip fabs: TSMC's fabs in Arizona and Intel's newest fab, with advanced packaging planned nearby.
site.abi.name: Texas
site.abi.what: Large new data centres for AI, where racks of accelerators are switched on and run for years.
site.spr.name: Spruce Pine
site.spr.what: A small town in North Carolina that mines most of the world's ultra-pure quartz, used for the crucibles silicon crystals are grown in.
site.gdl.name: Guadalajara
site.gdl.what: Servers and racks are assembled here, close to customers in the United States.
site.cam.name: Cambridge
site.cam.what: Arm designs instruction sets and processor cores used in nearly all phones and in a growing share of other chips. Chipmakers license them and build them into their own designs.
site.vel.name: Veldhoven
site.vel.what: ASML builds every EUV scanner in the world here, and many of the other scanners too. NXP, a large maker of car chips, is next door in Eindhoven.
site.obk.name: Oberkochen
site.obk.what: Zeiss grinds the mirrors inside every EUV scanner, among the smoothest large surfaces ever made.
site.obk.who: Zeiss SMT; Trumpf, near Stuttgart, builds the lasers that make EUV light
site.mun.name: Munich
site.mun.what: Infineon, one of the largest makers of chips for cars and power, has its headquarters here, and Siltronic makes silicon wafers.
site.stu.name: Stuttgart
site.stu.what: Bosch builds the control units that hold car chips, and makes chips of its own.
site.stu.who: Bosch; Mercedes-Benz and Porsche build cars here
site.dre.name: Dresden
site.dre.what: Europe's largest cluster of chip fabs, many making chips for cars and industry. A TSMC joint venture is being built here.
site.odz.name: Odesa
site.odz.what: Before 2022, firms here purified about half of the world's chip-grade neon, a gas for the lasers in deep-ultraviolet scanners.
site.isr.name: Israel
site.isr.what: Chip design centres for many companies, and Intel's fab at Kiryat Gat.
site.btu.name: Baotou
site.btu.what: China mines and refines most of the world's rare earths and makes almost all of its primary gallium, used in chips, magnets and tools.
site.btu.who: China Northern Rare Earth and others
site.sha.name: Shanghai
site.sha.what: China's chip hub: SMIC, its largest foundry, and many chip design companies, including some that design phone chips.
site.zz.name: Zhengzhou
site.zz.what: One of the largest phone factories in the world, where phones are put together from chips made elsewhere.
site.ich.name: Icheon
site.ich.what: South of Seoul, Samsung and SK hynix make much of the world's memory, including the stacked memory AI chips use. Samsung also makes chips for other companies.
site.tky.name: Tokyo
site.tky.what: Japan's makers of wafers, chemicals and tools: much of the world's silicon wafers and photoresist, coaters, testers, and the film inside high-end packages. Renesas, a large maker of car chips, is based here.
site.tky.who: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, Tokyo Electron, Advantest, JSR, Tokyo Ohka, Ajinomoto, Renesas
site.naka.name: Naka
site.naka.what: A Renesas fab that makes chips for cars. A fire here in March 2021 stopped a line for about a month, while carmakers were already short of chips.
site.kum.name: Kumamoto
site.kum.what: TSMC's joint venture with Sony and Denso has made chips here since 2024, and a second fab is being built.
site.hsc.name: Hsinchu
site.hsc.what: TSMC's headquarters and its newest fabs. Most of the world's most advanced chips are made here and in Tainan. MediaTek designs phone chips here.
site.tnn.name: Tainan
site.tnn.what: TSMC's largest advanced fabs, and lines that package chips side by side with their memory.
site.tpe.name: Taipei
site.tpe.what: Headquarters of the companies that build chips into servers, laptops and racks.
site.pen.name: Penang
site.pen.what: A centre of chip assembly and test since the 1970s: chips are cut, packaged and tested here for many companies.
site.pen.who: Intel, Infineon, Micron, ASE and others
site.sgp.name: Singapore
site.sgp.what: Fabs for mature chips and memory, and lines that test and package them.
site.chn.name: Chennai
site.chn.what: Phones are now assembled here too, as phone makers spread their factories beyond China.
page.build.lead: One open computer, and the record of how it gets built. Anyone, a person or an AI, can build a piece, break one that passed, or ask. An engine checks every entry; nobody votes.
page.build.studioD: Describe a piece, check it, see what the factory will do to it.
page.build.portD: Connect any AI agent to the lab's engines, to design with us.
page.build.joinD: Something the shared computer needs? Add it to the plan.
page.ecosystem.lead: No country makes a chip alone. Sand, machines, designs, factories and packaging come from different places, and every border is a risk.
page.ecosystem.mapD: Follow a data centre chip, a phone chip and a car chip across the world.
page.preview: The lab grows place by place: some levels are still flat drawings, waiting to be built in 3D.
page.challenges.lead: Every step of a chip's life has its challenges, each checked by a real engine. Finish one and something new grows on the island.
page.build.legend: Green is built, blue is yours, dashed is an open job, grey needs an engine to check it first. The loudest call comes first.
page.ecosystem.title: Beyond the island
page.questions.where: On the island, a question glows above every place. Inside a place, switch to Ask and they sit on the parts they are about.
page.questions.asked: Asked here, by people and agents
page.questions.none: Nobody has added a question yet. Follow one, and ask yours under it.
page.build.openD: Read from the ledger, not written by anyone: questions asked, designs nobody has broken, pieces nobody has built, checks nobody has written.
page.build.recordD: Every entry, the newest first. Nothing is changed or deleted: a design that turned out wrong stays, with the case that broke it.
page.build.mixD: If an AI can write a design in seconds, what do people bring? The ledger keeps count, as each entry says of itself.
page.build.society: Who is here, and what they do
page.build.societyD: Nobody was given a role. Each line is what one maker's entries add up to: what they build, whose work they checked, whose they built on. A program, an AI agent and a person each see different things; the record shows which.
page.build.empty: No person has added an entry yet. The agent's counter is waiting for its first break.
page.build.agent: Run an agent of your own
page.build.agentD: On your machine, under your name: a search program that attacks designs, or any AI through the open port. The lab runs none.
page.log.lead: Never a list of everything: these are the questions you have met and what you have done. Each leads on.

page.build.askK.one: A question from {by} · {n} piece of work so far
page.build.askK.other: A question from {by} · {n} pieces of work so far

read.title: Questions and challenges
read.lead: {n} questions about chips, each a page you can read with no picture. Some you can try now; others wait for an engine, a source or someone to build them. Start anywhere: every one leads to others.
read.none: No question has those words yet. Break it (⚑) to say which one is missing.
read.missing: There is no question at this address
read.secd.live: A challenge, a try or a piece of the shared computer is waiting on each, and an engine checks what you do.
read.secd.ready: An engine in the lab could already judge each of these. Nobody has built the way to try it yet.
read.secd.words: Only words so far: a question and something true to notice. No engine can check them yet.
read.secd.wanted: Each needs something the lab does not have: an engine nobody has written, or real cases and people from outside.
read.state.ready: An engine could check this; not built yet
read.state.wanted: Waits for something the lab doesn't have
read.noEngine: No engine checks this yet: what is true here rests on the notes and sources on this page.
read.wants.engine: It needs an engine nobody has written yet: {name}.
read.wants.part: Its engine, {name}, cannot work this out yet.
read.wants.outside: It needs something from outside the lab: real cases with sources, or people who have done it.
read.dirs: Directions that drop something chips take for granted
read.openNone: Nothing written here yet. What is open is yours to add.
read.by.strand: the same question, another way in
read.by.world: a question both of them serve
probe.tenfold: Each step along the bar is ten times more than the one before.
probe.cold.pump: Pumping its heat to the room
probe.all.says: A {n}-bit adder takes two numbers, so there are {pairs} pairs of inputs to try. Trying them all would take {time}.
probe.all.never: Nobody can wait that long. So big circuits are not proved right by trying every case: their designers prove them with logic, or test them in pieces small enough to try whole.
probe.all.can: That can be done. For a small circuit, trying every case is a real proof, and the lab's engines do it for every design you make.
probe.two.same: The engine tried both descriptions on all {rows} inputs: they give the same answers every time.
probe.two.slower: But they are not the same chip. One needs {a} switches, the other {b}, and the smaller one is slower: {da} picoseconds on its slowest path against {db}. Which one is right depends on what the chip is for.
probe.two.faster: But they are not the same chip. One needs {a} switches, the other {b}, and the smaller one is also faster: {da} picoseconds on its slowest path against {db}.
probe.two.tie: But they are not the same chip. One needs {a} switches, the other {b}, and both take {da} picoseconds on their slowest path: the smaller one costs less for the same speed.
probe.chain.one: A 1 went in, and after {n} parts it is still a clear 1.
probe.chain.zero: A 1 went in, and after {n} parts it reads as a 0. The answer is wrong.
probe.chain.unsure: A 1 went in, and after {n} parts nobody can tell whether it is a 1 or a 0.
probe.chain.whyRestore: Each part pushes a weak 1 back up to a full one before it can drift into the grey band, so the chain could go on for ever. Transistors do this; so must anything else that is to compute in long chains.
probe.chain.whyPass: Each part loses a little and adds a little noise, and nothing pushes the signal back. Whatever the parts are made of, without gain and a threshold a long chain cannot compute.
probe.chain.model: A model of the principle, not of any material: each part without gain keeps nine tenths of its signal, and the noise is the same every time you try, so you can compare. After R. W. Keyes, What makes a good computer device? (Science, 1985).
copies.aria: {n} copies of one design, from faster to slower, with the edge each must stay inside
copies.sample: The dots are a sample of {n} copies; the counts of what is accepted are the engine's, for every chip shipped.
walls.steps: Your chip stands {n} tenfold steps from this wall.
walls.at: Your chip is at the wall.
walls.past: Past the wall: this cannot be done this way.
walls.energySays: One multiply-and-add on your chip spends about {times} times the least energy physics allows for the bits it erases; {moving}% of it goes to moving the numbers, not to the arithmetic.
walls.tryingSays: To be sure of a {n}-bit adder by trying, you must try {pairs} pairs of inputs. A year of trying at a trillion a second covers {year}.
walls.doublingSays: For problems whose work doubles with each item, a chip {k} times faster handles only about {more} more items. Nobody has proved there is no cleverer way: it may be a wall, or a missing idea.
walls.settleSays: No program can tell, for every program, whether it will ever stop (Turing, 1936). No chip, however fast, comes any closer: there is no dot to move.
walls.softSays: Light was long thought unable to print details smaller than its own wavelength. 193-nanometre light went on to print features several times smaller, with water under the lens and patterns split over several exposures. A soft wall: it fell.
walls.how: Each track grows tenfold at every step toward its wall. The dots are placed by the Floor engine from your choices; the walls of physics and mathematics do not move.
walls.aria: Directions a chip could go, each with the wall at its end; choose one to see how far your chip stands from it
forms.errs: The engine cannot read {n} line(s) yet.
forms.state.errs: The description cannot be read yet ({n} problems).
forms.touch: Touch a signal (a, b, sum…) in any form, and it lights in all six.
forms.lit: {name} lit in every form: its words, its column, the gates that make it, their cells and wires.
forms.made.job: Written by a person: everything else is measured against it.
forms.made.descLab: Written by the lab. Change it, or write your own.
forms.made.descYou: Written by you: every form below follows as you type.
forms.made.does: Worked out by the engine on all {total} inputs: {bad} wrong.
forms.made.gates: Chosen by a program: {gates} gates, {tr} switches, slowest path {ps} ps.
forms.made.layout: Placed and wired by a program: {wire} units of wire, {vias} vias.
forms.made.masks: Made from the layout: one plate per layer; the whole process prints {n}.
forms.gatesAria: The design as {n} gates, from its inputs on the left to its outputs on the right
forms.how: Every form is the Design flow engine's, run again on each change: a 130-nanometre process, a small cell library, placement by simulated annealing, wires by a maze router. Two descriptions can give the same answers and be different chips: compare a right one with another right one.
forms.job.half: Add two bits, giving their sum and a carry. The first building block of every calculator and processor.
forms.job.vote: Output 1 when at least two of three inputs are 1. Spacecraft run three copies of a computer and trust the answer two of them agree on.
forms.job.full: Add three bits: a, b and the carry from the column to the right. Chained, adders like this add numbers of any size.
plan.aria: Your chip as a floor plan: its cores are busy {busy}% of the time
plan.waits: The cores ask for numbers faster than memory sends them: they work {busy}% of the time and wait the rest.
plan.fed: Memory keeps up: every core is fed.
plan.districtK: Give part of the floor to a special district
plan.share: How much of the job is its kind of work
plan.noDistrict: No special district: every core does every kind of work.
plan.pays: The district pays: the whole job runs {x} times faster than with general cores only.
plan.even: The district hardly matters: the whole job runs about as fast as with general cores only. The floor it takes and the work it speeds up cancel out.
plan.costs: The district costs: the job takes {x} times as long, because the space it takes is lost to the work it cannot do.
plan.how: Amdahl's law with a district, in the Work engine: in this model a special district does its one kind of work {k} times faster than the same area of general cores, and nothing else.
side.k: One job, every medium: a 1 passed down a chain of {n} parts
side.m.silicon.name: Silicon switches
side.m.silicon.what: a transistor and its wire, at 15 nm
side.m.loop.name: Superconducting loops
side.m.loop.what: a Josephson junction, kept colder than outer space
side.m.light.name: Light, handed on
side.m.light.what: a beam passed from part to part, with no gain
side.m.neuron.name: Neurons
side.m.neuron.what: a spike that sets off the next cell
side.m.dna.name: DNA strands
side.m.dna.what: one strand freeing the next, in a test tube
side.m.domino.name: Dominoes
side.m.domino.what: each one falling into the next
side.chainAria: {name}: the 1 along the chain, which ends as: {reads}
side.reset.fuel: used up: new strands for every go
side.pace: On screen, a step ten times longer adds {s} s to its lane: silicon finishes at once, DNA makes you wait.
side.kept: {k} of {n} keep the 1 over {len} parts: those whose parts restore it.
side.coolGone: Counted at the wall, the cold costs what the switching saved.
side.why: Every lane that keeps the 1 has gain and a threshold, whatever it is made of. What tells them apart is the rest: how long a step takes, what it costs, and who sets it back for the next go.
side.model: The curve and the noise are the Substrate engine's model of the principle, the same for every lane; each lane's energy and time are its own, from the sources above. The domino's are worked out: a 10 g domino 5 cm tall, 2 cm from the next, falling at the speed of a domino wave. Light's are missing on purpose: nobody has yet given a source for a light part that restores a 1.
side.bars: The blue bars are time for one step, from a tenth of a picosecond to hours; the orange, energy for one step, from zeptojoules to a tenth of a joule; each tenfold is the same length.
swm.k: A colony, no one in charge: ants between their nest and food, over a short bridge and a long one
swm.antsAria: Ants walking between a nest and food over a short bridge and a long one; the brighter a bridge, the more scent on it
swm.shareK: of the latest choices took the short bridge
swm.kill: Take away a third of the ants
swm.running: Each ant marks the bridge it walks and, at each end, picks a bridge by the scent on it. No ant knows which is shorter.
swm.waiting: Only the long bridge is open for now; the short one opens in {n} steps.
swm.v.short: The colony settled on the short bridge. No ant measured it: ants on it came back sooner, so its scent grew faster, and scent drew more ants. Run another colony: most settle on the short bridge, not all.
swm.v.long: This colony settled on the long bridge: early chance put more scent on it, and the lead grew on itself. A pattern nobody chose can be the wrong one.
swm.v.stuck: The short bridge opened, and the colony stayed on the long one: its trail was already there, and the trail held it. Argentine ants did the same when Goss and colleagues opened the shortcut late.
swm.v.ignore: No trail: ants that ignore scent split between the bridges, and the short one is no help.
swm.v.linear: No trail: when scent sways an ant only in proportion, neither bridge pulls ahead. Trails need ants that follow scent more than in proportion, as the measured ants do.
swm.v.fade: No trail: the scent fades faster than the ants lay it. A trail needs enough ants, or scent that lasts.
swm.killed: A third of the ants were taken away at step {t}; the trail is in the scent, not in any ant.
swm.late.1: later, once a trail has formed
swm.model: The rule is the one fitted to Argentine ants on a double bridge: the chance of a bridge grows with the square of (20 + the scent on it). Ants walk one step at a time; space, crowding and lost ants are left out.
swm.eyeK: The same idea in an eye: work only when news arrives
swm.cam: A camera reads every pixel, every frame
swm.ev: Eye-like pixels report only what changed
swm.camAria: The scene as a camera reads it, every pixel every frame
swm.evAria: The same scene through eye-like pixels: only the pixels that changed light up
swm.eye.none: Nothing moved. The camera still made {n} reads; the eye-like pixels said nothing at all.
swm.eye.some: The camera made {r} reads for every report of the eye-like pixels. The busier the scene, the closer they come.
swm.eyeModel: Each eye-like pixel reports when the light on it has changed by more than 15% since it last reported, as in an event camera.
tune.k: A box you cannot open: two dials on its face, a third nobody labelled, and a result that comes back with noise
tune.planeAria: The face of the box: dial 1 across, dial 2 up; {n} tries so far, each a patch coloured by its result
tune.start: Tap the face of the box to set both dials and run it. Dark means little came out; warm yellow means a lot.
tune.cold: Keep trying. Each try lights only the patch around it; the rest stays dark.
tune.warm: Something is there. Run the same setting again: does it give the same number?
tune.hot: A good result. Is it the setting, or was this run lucky? The box changes a little each time it runs.
tune.reset: Start over with a new box
tune.openFound: Your first truly good setting came at try {n} (its true result: {q}).
tune.openNot: None of your tries was truly good yet (the best was {q}).
tune.openSay: Real machines do not open. This is what your tries could not show you: the true result at the unlabelled dial's setting, without noise.
tune.noteK: Write it down for someone else
tune.noteWait: Try the box first; a note needs something learned.
tune.noteSet: The setting in your note: dial 1 at {a}, dial 2 at {b}, the unlabelled dial at {c}.
tune.words: Anything else you would tell them
tune.wordsPh: what you noticed, what fooled you, what to try first…
tune.h.twin: Your note, on the twin box
tune.median: half found a good setting within {n} tries; {s}% found one at all
tune.notFound: fewer than half found a good setting in {b} tries ({s}% did)
tune.s.noteFaster: Your note carried: from it the program needed about {n} tries, against {c} from nothing.
tune.s.noteOnly: Your note carried: from it the program needed about {n} tries; from nothing, most runs never got there.
tune.s.noteNoHelp: Your note did not help much here: about {n} tries from it, {c} from nothing.
tune.s.noteFail: From your note, most runs never found a good setting: the note pointed somewhere the box no longer gives its best, or never did.
tune.s.twinWorse: On the twin, the same note took about {w} tries: the same kind of box, small hidden differences, much to learn again.
tune.s.twinOk: On the twin, about {w} tries: here the note still carried.
tune.s.twinFail: On the twin, most runs never got there: the same kind of box, small hidden differences, and the note led them astray.
tune.wordsLost: Your words went nowhere: the program reads only the setting and how far you trust it. A person reading them might have done better, or not.
tune.model: The box is the Tune engine: not a model of any real machine, recipe or factory, but of learning by trying. Two dials work only together, a second-best patch can hold you, the unlabelled dial moves everything, every run has noise, the box drifts a little each time it runs, and its twin is set a little differently. Every shape is chosen; someone who has run a real process should check it, and until then it is a draft. The program is a simple search that keeps a step when it gives a better number; its results are over {runs} runs, each of {b} tries, and a setting counts as good from {good} out of 100.
machines.ui.go: Pick a need, and build a machine for it from shared blocks, with an agent beside you
machines.ui.title: What would you build if machines were assembled from shared blocks, for one person and one need?
machines.ui.lead: There is no standard computer here. Pick a need, then choose the form of each block: as software it can change at any time, as a circuit it runs far cheaper but is fixed once made, as liquid hardware it is a fabric rewired after it is made, and as new matter it is made of something beyond today's chip. Or let an agent assemble it, and decide for yourself.
machines.ui.energy: the energy of the same machine made all as circuits
machines.ui.changes: parts that can still change after it is made
machines.ui.reset: Start again: every part a circuit
machines.ui.agentLead: The agent tries every way to make this machine, in every place it could be made, keeps those that follow the grammar and meet the need, and shows the ones no other beats on energy, change, exactness and days a try at once. It decides nothing.
machines.ui.tried: Tried {tried} machines: {valid} pass, and {front} are beaten by no other.
machines.ui.decide: Which one is right depends on what the machine is for. That is your call, not the agent's.
machines.ui.blocksLead: What everyone shares instead of a standard machine: what flows in and out of each block, the forms it can take, and how it is checked.
machines.ui.note: How it is scored: for the same work, software costs about 500 times a circuit made for it (a general-purpose chip against a custom one for video, Hameed et al.), and new matter costs what its claims say, from in products down to guesses, shown as a range and never below the energy floor. Each part's share of the work is a choice of the model, so the energy is always this machine against itself, never in joules.
machines.rule.kind: {part}: a wire joins two different kinds of port
machines.rule.fed: {part} has an input that nothing feeds
machines.rule.core: {part} runs as software, but no core made as a circuit is there to run it
machines.miss.change: {part} must still change after the machine is made: make it software or new matter
machines.miss.exact: {part} must be exact, and new matter is not
machines.check.open: Open in the community's plan: anyone can design it
machines.check.partly: Partly built in the community's plan
machines.check.engine: Waits for an engine that can check it
machines.check.lab: Checked by one of the lab's engines
machines.block.sensor.d: Turns a signal from the world, such as sound, smoke or light, into numbers.
machines.block.learner.d: Numbers in, numbers out, shaped by numbers it has learned: a filter, a detector, a guide.
machines.block.memory.d: Keeps numbers until they are needed.
machines.block.counter.d: Counts ticks: a clock for when to wake up and what to do next.
machines.block.voter.d: Three copies answer and the majority wins, so one fault cannot change the result.
machines.block.parity.d: Says whether a number arrived with one bit flipped.
machines.block.core.d: A RISC-V core: it runs any block given to it as software.
machines.need.hearing.d: Tiny, all day on one small battery
machines.need.hearing.why: Its filter has to be tuned to each person's hearing, so it must still change after the machine is made.
machines.need.wildfire.d: Ten years in a forest, no service
machines.need.wildfire.why: Nothing has to change once it is out there: what matters most is the battery.
machines.need.rover.d: Far away, cold, hit by radiation
machines.need.rover.why: Its guide has to take updates from Earth, and its voter and core must be exact, because radiation flips bits out there.
invent.ui.lead: New matter may not exist yet, so every kind rests on claims, and every claim says how sure it is twice: whether anyone has built it (in products, shown in a lab, a guess) and how the lab knows it (an idea drawn, real numbers, computed). Tap a mark for what it means. Guesses are allowed and labelled; physics sets the floor.
invent.ui.none: No part is made of new matter yet. Choose the hexagon on a part that can take it to see the claims behind each kind.
invent.ui.range: If the guesses hold: {low} the energy of a circuit. If they fail: {high}.
invent.matter.cim.d: Numbers held and multiplied where they are stored.
invent.matter.light.d: Multiplies by sending light through a mesh of tiny tunable splitters.
invent.matter.spikes.d: Neurons that fire only when something happens, as in a brain.
invent.matter.reversible.d: Logic that can run backwards and take back the energy of each step.
invent.matter.living.d: Lab-grown neurons on a chip that learn, kept alive.
invent.claim.cimArray: A crossbar multiplies where the numbers are stored; its energy, converters included, comes from the lab's compute-in-memory engine.
invent.claim.cimNoise: No two devices are quite alike, so the answers are close, not exact.
invent.claim.lightReal: Processors that compute with light are installed in research computing centres.
invent.claim.lightNoise: Light drifts in phase, so the answers are close, not exact.
invent.claim.lightCheap: Multiplying in light costs a tenth of what a circuit spends.
invent.claim.lightConvert: Turning numbers into light and back costs twice what the light saves.
invent.claim.spikesReal: Spiking systems with over a billion neurons have been built.
invent.claim.spikesEvents: A spiking part spends energy only when something happens, so a quiet need costs little.
invent.claim.spikesCost: Each spike costs three times a circuit's step.
invent.claim.revChip: A reversible test chip took back part of its energy: the same logic used about 30% less.
invent.claim.revFree: Taken back almost completely, a step would cost almost nothing.
invent.claim.liveReal: A computer with living neurons on a chip is on sale today.
invent.claim.liveBrain: Living neurons compute as cheaply as a brain, which runs on about 20 watts.
invent.claim.liveSupport: Keeping the cells alive costs a hundred times what they save.
invent.wall.floor: A claim hit the floor: no step can cost less than erasing the bits it must erase, so the guess stops there.
machines.rule.fab: {part} cannot be made where you chose: pick another place, or another form
machines.ui.days: days for one try: from a design to a part to test
machines.ui.intoCore: Go into the core: watch it run this machine's job
invent.claim.liveGrown: Grown from cells, not made in a fab: how long a try takes is not known.
machines.miss.keep: {part} must reshape as fast as its job changes, and this form is too slow
machines.need.radio.d: The signals around it change in nanoseconds
machines.need.radio.why: The signals it hunts change faster than most hardware can be rewired: finding them and pulling them out must reshape every 100 nanoseconds, and pulling them out must be exact.
machines.ui.modes: Look at the machine, or play its challenge
machines.ui.runsOn: runs as software on the core
machines.ui.partsLead: Tap a block on the machine, or a part here, and choose its form.
machines.ui.tap: Tap a block on the machine to change its form.
machines.ui.must.change: must still change after it is made
machines.rib.every: a part that must change has to keep up
machines.rib.reshape: How long each part takes to change once it is made
machines.rib.blocks: Each block shows what flows into it and out of it
machines.front.aria: Energy against how many parts can still change: the agent's offers, today's best compromises, and your machine
machines.front.x: Across: energy against all circuits, less to the left
machines.front.y: Up: parts that can still change
machines.front.offers: Dots: the agent's offers, filled when every part is exact
machines.front.broken: Dashed ring: your machine, which does not work yet
machines.front.wait: Let the agent assemble it, and its offers draw today's best compromises here.
machines.do.least.t: Keep its rules with the least energy
machines.do.least.d: Follow the grammar, keep every rule of the need, and spend as little energy as any machine can. Only what is in products or shown in a lab counts.
machines.do.week.t: The least energy, with a try within a week
machines.do.week.d: Every try must come back within a week, even if a guess fails, so the machine can be tried again and again. Still the least energy you can.
machines.do.exact.t: The least energy, with more parts exact
machines.do.exact.d: A part that answers only roughly cannot be trusted here: every part marked with equals must be exact too. Still the least energy you can.
machines.do.miss.exact: {part} must be exact for this goal
machines.do.miss.days: A try takes more than a week
machines.do.won: Won: no machine that keeps this goal spends less.
machines.do.hint.hearing.least: The filter must still change after it is made, and a circuit cannot. Of the forms that can change, which costs least? The claims of each kind of new matter say how sure it is.
machines.do.why.hearing.least: Memory that computes multiplies where the numbers are kept, so the filter costs a small part of a circuit's energy and can still be retuned. Its answers are close, not exact, which a hearing aid can live with.
machines.do.hint.hearing.week: Memory that computes is made only in a giant fab, and a try there takes months. Which form that can change is bought ready-made instead?
machines.do.why.hearing.week: A fabric rewired by bits is bought and configured, so a try takes a day. It costs more than memory that computes, but a new filter can be tried every day.
machines.do.hint.wildfire.least: Nothing has to change out there, so every part may be fixed. The detector does most of the work, but the check and the clock count too. Which forms spend least, counting only what is shown?
machines.do.why.wildfire.least: Memory that computes does the detector's work for a sliver of the energy, and reversible logic takes back part of what the check and the clock spend.
machines.do.hint.wildfire.week: A giant fab takes months for one try. The forms can stay as they are: where else could the circuits be made?
machines.do.why.wildfire.week: A flexible line prints circuits on plastic in days. The energy here is counted as if made at the finest lines, so try here, then make the winner in a giant fab.
machines.do.hint.rover.least: The guide must take updates from Earth; the voter and the core must be exact. Which forms keep those rules and spend least?
machines.do.why.rover.least: Memory that computes runs the guide for little and can still be updated, and reversible logic is exact, so the voter and the clock can take back part of their energy and still be trusted.
machines.do.hint.rover.exact: Now the guide must be exact as well as changeable. New matter that changes is not exact: what else can change and stay exact?
machines.do.why.rover.exact: A fabric rewired by bits is exact like a circuit and can still take updates from Earth. It costs more, so the rest is made as cheap as the rules allow.
machines.do.hint.radio.least: Finding a signal and pulling it out must reshape as fast as the signals change. Open the layer of how fast each part reshapes to see which form keeps up.
machines.do.why.radio.least: An array rewired on every tick of the clock keeps up, shown in a lab. Its energy is a guess, so it counts as an FPGA's until someone shows it; a reversible clock saves a little more.
machines.do.hint.radio.week: The reversible clock waits months on a giant fab. What else could the clock be, made where a try takes days?
machines.do.why.radio.week: With the clock a plain circuit printed on a flexible line, a try takes days, for almost the same energy.
liquid.kind.fpga.d: An FPGA: a grid of tiny lookup tables and switches, rewired by loading a new configuration.
liquid.kind.cgra.d: A coarse-grained array: small arithmetic units whose wiring changes on every tick of the clock.
liquid.kind.goal.d: The goal: a fabric that reshapes in 50 nanoseconds at nearly a circuit's energy.
liquid.note.fpgaArea: About 35 times the area of a custom chip for the same logic, and 3.4 to 4.6 times slower.
liquid.note.fpgaWhole: Rewiring the whole chip took 3.8 seconds; rewiring part of it, 209 milliseconds, or 324 microseconds through the chip's own port.
liquid.note.cgraChip: A test chip had 28.6 times the power efficiency of an FPGA platform; against a circuit made for the job, no source gives one figure.
liquid.note.goalAim: DARPA's aim: processors that reconfigure within 50 nanoseconds. Nobody has shown it yet.
liquid.ui.lead: A fabric rewired after it is made: exact like a circuit, changeable like software. It pays in energy for the switches that make it flexible, and in the time it takes to rewire, when it does no work.
liquid.ui.mapAria: How fast each part of this machine can reshape, against its energy compared with a circuit made for the job
liquid.ui.corner: fast to reshape and costs like a circuit: nothing is there yet
liquid.ui.everyKey: parts that must change have to be right of the line
liquid.ui.none: No part is liquid yet. Choose the drop on a part that is logic to see the fabrics.
liquid.ui.energy: {x} the energy of a circuit made for the job
liquid.ui.fallback: If the guesses fail, a guessed fabric is no better than an FPGA: its energy and its time to rewire.
liquid.ui.evolve: When a fabric rewires itself, who designed it? In 1996 evolution rewired an FPGA to tell two tones apart, and the circuit worked in ways nobody could fully explain.
mb.trip.intro: Send one bit from memory to the arithmetic and watch what it costs. Then move the memory: on the chip, stacked on it, beside it, across the board, or in another machine reached by light.
mb.trip.look: Fetch two numbers: {f}. Add them: {a}. {k}× more to fetch.
mb.trip.wireShare: {v} of the bit's energy is spent on the way, not in the memory
mb.trip.note: Energies from the same 45 nm table as Follow the joule: right in direction and share, high for today's chips. Capacity counts every wire; money is the price of a gigabyte kept there.
mb.at.near.d: Memory on the same chip (SRAM, fast memory built from switches), a millimetre from the arithmetic: cheap to reach, but it takes costly chip area.
mb.at.stacked.d: Memory stacked straight on top of the chip and joined through thousands of tiny vertical wires: short and wide, but the heat has further to go.
mb.at.beside.d: A stack of memory chips beside the processor in the same package (HBM), joined by thousands of wires through a silicon bridge.
mb.at.board.d: Memory chips on the circuit board, about ten centimetres away: few wires, and every bit is pushed out of one chip and into another.
mb.at.rack.d: Memory in another machine two metres away, reached through a fibre: light costs the same few picojoules whether it goes a metre or a hundred, but it adds time.

mb.wall.lightD.one: At light's own speed this trip lasts {n} tick of a 3 GHz clock; the bit takes {m}.
mb.wall.lightD.other: At light's own speed this trip lasts {n} ticks of a 3 GHz clock; the bit takes {m}.

mb.wall.kLight.one: At light's own speed the pantry is {n} of the chef's ticks away; a fetch takes {m}.
mb.wall.kLight.other: At light's own speed the pantry is {n} of the chef's ticks away; a fetch takes {m}.

mb.wall.shannonD: One wire carries {r}; its noise allows at most {c}, whatever the design.
mb.wall.floorD: Moving this bit costs {x} times the least that writing one bit can cost.
mb.wall.kFloor: A bit from the pantry costs {e}, {x} times the least that writing one bit can cost.
mb.k.intro: Each round the chef cooks faster; the pantry hardly speeds up. Pull the levers, then serve five rounds. A level is cleared when, in the last round, the chef waits no more than the goal and an answer costs no more energy than it allows.
mb.k.aria: {level}, round {r}: the chef waits {wait} of the time; {e} an answer.
mb.k.note: A small model, fair enough to compare plans and never wrong in direction: the chef grows faster as processors did against memory (Wulf and McKee, 1995); prices and sizes are the model's own. Every lever's catch is in the engine, src/engines/bits.js.
mb.lv.wire.q: Fetching two numbers costs far more than adding them. Why?
mb.lv.wire.who: The chef is a chip's arithmetic; the pantry is memory on the far side of the same chip, a wire away.
mb.lv.chip.q: Why does a faster chip spend more of its time waiting for data?
mb.lv.chip.who: The chef is a processor; the pantry is memory chips across the board.
mb.lv.stacked.q: What if the work were brought to the data: memory stacked on the chip, or cooking inside it?
mb.lv.stacked.who: The chef is an AI chip; the pantry is a stack of memory beside it in the package.
mb.lv.light.q: Past some distance a wire loses to light. Where is that distance?
mb.lv.light.who: The chef is a processor; the pantry is a pool of memory a metre away, in another box.
mb.lv.dc.q: AI chips sit idle much of the time, waiting for numbers. How much of that wait can be won back?
mb.lv.dc.who: The chef is an AI chip answering one person: every number of the model is read once for each word it writes, and used once.
mb.lv.brain.q: A brain's signals crawl compared with a chip's, yet it thinks quickly on very little power. How does it keep its wires short?
mb.lv.brain.who: The chef is a group of neurons; the pantry is what other parts of the brain hold, a nerve fibre away.
mb.lv.team.q: Everyone on a team knows something. Why does sharing it take so long, and what helps?
mb.lv.team.who: The chef is a person at work; the pantry is what a colleague across the building knows.
mb.lever.closer.catch: Less room: memory on the chip takes space from the chef.
mb.lever.wider.catch: More wires and more money, and the chip's edge holds only so many.
mb.lever.shelf.catch: A cache must guess what comes next; a wrong guess fetches for nothing.
mb.lever.stack.t: Stack the pantry on the kitchen
mb.lever.stack.catch: The heat is harder to get out, so the chef slows down.
mb.lever.light.catch: Turning bits into light and back costs energy, near or far.
mb.lever.cim.catch: Computing in memory: the answers become approximate.
mb.lever.closer.brainC: Cells packed together leave less room for others.
mb.lever.wider.brainC: Every fibre costs room and energy to keep.
mb.lever.shelf.brainC: A local memory must guess what will be needed.
mb.lever.stack.brainC: A tighter fold is harder to cool.
mb.lever.light.brainC: Signals race along, but the wrapping costs room to grow.
mb.lever.cim.brainC: Answers come out roughly right, not exact.
mb.lever.closer.team: Sit near the people you ask
mb.lever.closer.teamC: Desks near one team are far from another.
mb.lever.wider.teamC: More people in the room cost more hours.
mb.lever.shelf.teamC: Notes must guess what will be asked; most are never read.
mb.lever.stack.teamC: The noise slows everyone down a little.
mb.lever.light.teamC: Every call takes minutes to set up.
mb.lever.cim.team: Let the one who knows do it
mb.lever.cim.teamC: It gets done their way, not quite as asked.
mb.say.ready: Pull the levers, then serve: five rounds, the chef faster each time.
mb.say.ok: Kept busy: in the last round the chef waits {wait} of the time, and an answer costs {e}. Level cleared.
mb.say.wait: In the last round the chef waits {wait} of the time: the pantry cannot keep up.
mb.say.energy: The chef is busy enough, but an answer costs {e}: too much of it goes on moving bits.
mb.say.money: This kitchen costs more than the level can spend.
mb.say.space: The door needs more wires than the chip's edge can hold.
mb.say.error: Cooking in the pantry gives answers too rough for this level.
mb.hint: Try {lever}: {v}. The nearest plan that works changes {n} levers.
mb.keep.lead: Keep this plan in the ledger: the engine scores it, and it joins this level's curve of the best time waiting.
mb.curve.aria: {n} attempts kept at {level}: the time the chef waits, and the best so far.
mb.curve.d: {n} attempts kept here; the best so far waits {best} of the time.
mb.curve.none: Nobody has kept an attempt here yet.
invent.status.product.line: In products: something built this way can be bought or is in use today.
invent.status.lab.line: Shown in a lab: someone has made it work, but nobody sells it yet.
invent.status.guess.line: A guess: nobody has shown it yet. Its number is written down so it can be argued with.
